title: PAUL ASKED WHY CHRISTIANS WERE JOINING THEIR BODIES TO PROSTITUTES
paragraphs: PAUL ASKED WHY CHRISTIANS WERE JOINING THEIR BODIES TO PROSTITUTES
What Paul said next in 1 Corinthians 6 was not merely a warning about sex. It was a devastating reminder that Jesus did not redeem your soul while leaving your body behind.
There are Bible passages we like to frame.
There are Bible passages we like to underline.
And then there are Bible passages that seem to reach through the page, put a hand on the secret part of our lives, and ask a question we desperately hoped nobody would ever ask.
First Corinthians 6 is one of those passages.
Paul is writing to Christians.
Not pagans outside the church.
Not people who had never heard the Gospel.
Christians.
People who confessed Jesus.
People who had been washed.
People who had been sanctified.
People Paul could remind, only a few sentences earlier, that their former lives did not have to define them anymore:
“καὶ ταῦτά τινες ἦτε” — kai tauta tines ēte.
“And such were some of you.”
Were.
That little word carries an ocean of grace.

Paul does not pretend Corinth has a spotless past. He openly names sexual sin, idolatry, adultery, greed, drunkenness, abusive speech and exploitation. Then he turns toward people whose histories were anything but clean and essentially says:
That was you.
But something happened.
You were washed.
You were sanctified.
You were justified in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ and by the Spirit of our God.
That is the atmosphere in which we must read what comes next. Paul is not throwing stones at sexually broken people from a safe religious distance.
He is speaking to redeemed people who are in danger of forgetting what redemption means.
And then he asks a question so uncomfortable that almost two thousand years later, Christians still feel its force.
“οὐκ οἴδατε ὅτι τὰ σώματα ὑμῶν μέλη Χριστοῦ ἐστιν;”
Ouk oidate hoti ta sōmata hymōn melē Christou estin?
“Do you not know that your bodies are members of Christ?”
Then comes the shock.
“ἄρας οὖν τὰ μέλη τοῦ Χριστοῦ ποιήσω πόρνης μέλη;”
Should I take the members of Christ and make them members of a prostitute?
Paul answers:
“μὴ γένοιτο.”
Mē genoito.
Absolutely not.
May it never be.

The Greek text is unmistakably physical. Paul uses sōmata—bodies. He uses melē—members, parts belonging to a larger whole. He uses pornēs, from pornē—a prostitute. His argument is not that the human body is dirty.
It is almost exactly the opposite.
Your body matters so much that Paul connects what you do with it to your union with Christ.
And suddenly this ancient letter becomes painfully modern.
Because we have become experts at dividing ourselves.
Sunday belongs to Jesus.
Monday belongs to ambition.
The prayer life belongs to Jesus.
The browser history belongs to us.
The worship belongs to Jesus.
The private messages belong to us.
The Bible app belongs to Jesus.
The hidden folder belongs to us.
The public Christian identity belongs to Jesus.
The secret appetite...
well...
we tell ourselves that is nobody else's business.
Paul destroys that illusion.
Your body is not a spiritual side issue.
Your sexuality is not disconnected from your discipleship.
What happens behind a locked door does not become spiritually meaningless simply because nobody from church can see it.
And what happens on a screen can still train the desires of a real human heart.
Maybe nobody knows.
Maybe your spouse does not know.
Maybe your parents do not know.
Maybe your pastor does not know.
Maybe the people who read your Christian posts would never imagine it.
Maybe you have become so skilled at deleting the evidence that even you have started pretending there is nothing left to confess.
But there is Someone in the room.
Christ.
That is what makes Paul's argument so piercing.
He does not merely ask, “Why are you doing something immoral?”
He asks something deeper:
Have you forgotten whose you are?
Paul continues:
“ὁ κολλώμενος τῇ πόρνῃ ἓν σῶμά ἐστιν.”
The one joined to a prostitute is one body with her.
Then Paul reaches all the way back to Genesis:
“The two will become one flesh.”
And immediately he places beside that another reality:
“ὁ δὲ κολλώμενος τῷ κυρίῳ ἓν πνεῦμά ἐστιν.”
Ho de kollōmenos tō Kyriō hen pneuma estin.
The one joined to the Lord is one spirit with Him.
Notice the repeated word behind “joined”: kollaō.
To join.
To attach.
To cling.
Paul wants the Corinthians to understand that sex cannot simply be reduced to appetite.
The culture may say, “It is only physical.”
Paul says your physical life belongs inside a much larger spiritual reality.
The culture says, “It is my body.”
Paul is about to answer:
Not ultimately.
The culture says, “Nobody got hurt.”
Paul asks whether we have considered what sin does to the person committing it.
The culture says, “Follow the desire.”
Paul says:
“φεύγετε τὴν πορνείαν.”
Pheugete tēn porneian.
“Flee sexual immorality.”
Not negotiate with it.
Not keep it close enough to enjoy but far enough away to maintain plausible deniability.
Not see how near you can stand before falling.
Flee.
Sometimes the most spiritual thing you can do is close the tab.
Delete the number.
End the secret conversation.
Walk out of the room.
Cancel the rendezvous.
Put the phone somewhere else.
Confess to a mature believer who will actually hold you accountable.
Stop calling bondage “a struggle” when you have quietly arranged your life so the temptation always has an unlocked door.
There are temptations Scripture tells us to resist.
Here, Paul tells us to run.
And somebody reading this knows exactly why.
You have promised God before.
“Never again.”
Then again happened.
You cried.
You repented.
You felt clean for three days.
Seven days.
Maybe three months.
Then loneliness came.
Or anger.
Or rejection.
Or boredom.
Or opportunity.
The screen lit up.
The old person messaged.
The memory returned.
The fantasy began.
And somewhere between temptation and surrender, you heard that terrible whisper:
You have already failed before.
What difference does one more time make?
A tremendous difference.
Not because one more failure makes you unreachable.
But because the voice telling you to surrender is lying about who owns you.
Listen to Paul.
“καὶ οὐκ ἐστὲ ἑαυτῶν.”
Kai ouk este heautōn.
“You are not your own.”
Then:
“ἠγοράσθητε γὰρ τιμῆς.”
Ēgorasthēte gar timēs.
“You were bought with a price.”
And therefore:
“δοξάσατε δὴ τὸν θεὸν ἐν τῷ σώματι ὑμῶν.”
Doxasate dē ton Theon en tō sōmati hymōn.
“Therefore glorify God in your body.”
There it is.
The Gospel underneath the command.
You were bought.
Paul does not say, “Clean yourself up so Jesus might consider purchasing you.”
Bought.
The transaction precedes the command.
Grace precedes obedience.
Redemption becomes the foundation of holiness.

Christ's claim upon the Christian is not the claim of an abusive master purchasing disposable property. It is the claim of the Redeemer who gave Himself to rescue sinners and now calls those redeemed people to live as people who belong to Him.
You were bought with a price.
What price?
Paul does not spell it out in this particular verse, but the center of his Gospel leaves no mystery about the direction of his thought.
Jesus Christ gave Himself.
The Son of God went to the cross.
The sinless One bore judgment for sinners.
The blood was real.
The nails were real.
The suffering was real.
The death was real.
And the resurrection was real.

In fact, resurrection is already part of Paul's argument in this very passage: God raised the Lord and will also raise believers by His power. That means Christianity does not treat your body as temporary garbage while God cares only about an invisible soul.
God intends resurrection.
Your body matters to Him.
And that changes the question.
The question is no longer merely:
“How much can I get away with and still call myself Christian?”
The question becomes:
“How can this body, purchased by Christ, glorify the One who purchased me?”
Your eyes can glorify God.
Your hands can glorify God.
Your sexuality can glorify God.
Your singleness can glorify God.
Your marriage can glorify God.
Your phone can be handled in a way that glorifies God.
Your bedroom can glorify God.
Your private decisions can glorify God.
Your refusal can glorify God.
Your repentance can glorify God.
Even the body in which you once sinned can become the body through which you now obey.
That is grace.
And perhaps the most beautiful part of this chapter is hidden just before all of these warnings.
Paul had already told them:
“And such were some of you.”
Some of you were sexually immoral.
Some of you were adulterers.
Some of you were greedy.
Some of you were drunkards.
Some of you exploited people.
But—
you were washed.
You were sanctified.
You were justified.
Paul can confront their sin fiercely because he believes Christ can transform sinners completely.
Christianity is not the announcement that respectable people should congratulate themselves for being cleaner than everyone else.
It is the announcement that guilty people can be washed.
The prostitute needs Jesus.
The person visiting the prostitute needs Jesus.
The pornography addict needs Jesus.
The adulterer needs Jesus.
The virgin needs Jesus.
The married person needs Jesus.
The sexually disciplined person needs Jesus.
The person who fell last night needs Jesus.
The person who has been walking faithfully for twenty years still needs Jesus.
Nobody reaches the cross with clean hands.
We come because we need mercy.
And there is something especially dangerous about Christians discussing sexual sin as though the only people who need repentance are “those people out there.”
Paul was writing to the church.
That should humble us.
The church can sing while hiding.
Preach while hiding.
Serve while hiding.
Lead while hiding.
Smile for photographs while hiding.
Post Scripture while hiding.
And hiding can become so normal that exposure begins to feel more frightening than bondage.
But Jesus did not die so that you could become better at hiding.
He died to bring sinners into the light.
There is a difference between conviction and condemnation.
Condemnation whispers:
“You are filthy. Run away from God.”
Biblical conviction says:
“This is sin. Run toward Christ.”
Condemnation tells you your failure is your identity.
The Gospel tells repentant believers that sin must be confessed and forsaken precisely because Christ has given them a new identity.
That is why the words immediately preceding this passage matter so much:
“And such were some of you.”
Were.
Maybe that word needs to become personal tonight.
Pornography does not have to write the final chapter.
Adultery does not have to write the final chapter.
Promiscuity does not have to write the final chapter.
Sexual compromise does not have to write the final chapter.
Your worst night does not have to become the title over the rest of your life.
The cross is where scandal meets grace.
Not cheap grace.
Not grace that tells sin it does not matter.
Grace powerful enough to call sin what God calls it and still open the door for the sinner to come home.
Grace that forgives.
Grace that cleanses.
Grace that teaches us to say no.
Grace that gets into the places we thought would always remain chained.
Grace that does not merely improve the scandal.
Grace rewrites the story.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Maybe you have been asking God to remove the consequences when what He wants first is your surrender.
Maybe you have been asking Him to make temptation disappear while protecting the very access points through which temptation keeps entering.
Maybe you want freedom without confession.
Restoration without repentance.
Victory without fleeing.
Jesus loves you too much to cooperate with the version of Christianity that lets you keep your chains as souvenirs.
Bring the hidden thing into the light.
Not because confession purchases forgiveness.
Christ purchased redemption.
But genuine repentance stops defending the darkness and turns toward God.
Tell Jesus the truth.
He already knows.

If another person has been sinned against, biblical repentance may also require truth, responsibility, wisdom, restitution where appropriate, and a willingness to face consequences rather than using “grace” as an escape hatch.

And if your sexual history includes coercion, abuse, exploitation, or something done to you against your will, do not twist Paul's words into an accusation against yourself. Someone else's sin against your body is not your moral guilt. Seek wise pastoral and professional help where needed. Christ's compassion is not reserved for people whose wounds are simple.
But if this passage is exposing something you chose...
do not scroll quickly because you feel ashamed.
Stay here.
Not with me.
With Christ.
You are not being invited merely to feel terrible.
You are being invited to repent.
Those are not the same thing.
Judas regretted.
Peter wept and returned.
The Gospel does not merely produce people who hate what they have done.
It produces people who turn toward the Savior.
So turn.
Even if your voice shakes.
Even if you have prayed this prayer before.
Even if you are ashamed that you are still fighting something you thought you would have conquered years ago.
Turn again.
Jesus Christ is still the Savior of sinners.
And if you belong to Him, your battle for holiness is not an attempt to persuade Him to love you.
It is the response of someone who has been bought with a price.
Maybe tonight your prayer is only:

“Jesus, I have been treating as mine what You purchased. Forgive me. Clean me. Teach me to flee what dishonors You. Take my eyes, my thoughts, my desires, my relationships, my sexuality, my habits, my phone, my loneliness, my body. I belong to You.”
If this exposed something hidden, you do not have to describe your sin publicly. But you do not have to pretend either.
Let somebody know there is a real human being behind the screen who still wants Jesus more than the chains.
And if Christ has already brought you out of sexual bondage, shame, adultery, pornography, or another hidden prison, perhaps your comment should be:
Your testimony might become the reason somebody else realizes failure does not have to be final.
Not because an article can save you.
Only Christ saves.
Come back to Paul's words:
You are not your own.
You were bought with a price.
Glorify God in your body.
Not as a performance of spirituality. Not as a way of earning favor with God.
Send it privately to the believer who has been drifting.
And yes, send it to the person who does not yet believe, because Christianity's message is not “good people save themselves.”
It is that Jesus Christ saves sinners.
But voluntary support can help Christian teaching and discipleship resources continue reaching people who might otherwise never encounter them.
But the deepest reason to stay connected is not merchandise.
It is discipleship.
Invite the friend who is struggling.
Invite the believer who has gone cold.
Invite the seeker with questions.
Invite the person who has not opened a Bible in years.
Even invite the unbeliever who thinks Christians only know how to condemn broken people.
Let them encounter the scandalous message at the center of Christianity:
Sin is more serious than we wanted to admit.
Grace is greater than we dared to believe.
And Jesus is better than the chains we keep running back to.
Paul's words remain uncomfortable because they refuse to let us reduce Christianity to something that happens inside our thoughts.
Your body belongs to Christ.
Your private life matters.
Your choices matter.
Holiness matters.
But underneath every command stands something even more breathtaking.
A price was paid.
Christ did not look at ruined sinners and walk away.
He came for them.
He died for them.
He rose again.
And those who belong to Him are no longer required to live as prisoners of the person they used to be.
“And such were some of you.”
Maybe one day somebody will describe the sin currently tormenting you...
and by the grace of Jesus Christ, you will be able to whisper:
That was me.
That was who I was.
But Jesus found me there.
Jesus forgave me there.
Jesus began changing me there.
I thought my scandal had already written the ending.
Then grace picked up the pen.
The sin you thought would become your final chapter may become the very place where future generations see just how completely Jesus Christ can rewrite a human life.
